title: Show HN: Directory of 28 AI crawlers – robots.txt rules, IP ranges, open data
content:
The bot directory · 28 crawlers · refreshed monthly
Every AI crawler, explained
This is a maintained directory of the AI bots and user agents that crawl the web — the crawlers behind ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, Gemini, and the training datasets feeding every major model. Each profile explains what the bot does, whether it actually respects robots.txt, and gives copy-paste rules to allow or block it. To check what your own robots.txt currently permits, run the AI Crawler Access Checker.

Commonly confused pairs
- GPTBot vs OAI-SearchBotBlocking one does not block the other — training and ChatGPT search are separate opt-outs.
- GPTBot vs ChatGPT-UserOne crawls the open web for training; the other fetches a single page because a person asked ChatGPT to look at it.
- OAI-SearchBot vs ChatGPT-UserBoth serve ChatGPT, but one builds the index ahead of time and the other fetches live, per request.
- ClaudeBot vs Claude-UserAnthropic split training from user-triggered fetching across two agents; blocking the wrong one has the opposite effect from the one intended.
- ClaudeBot vs Claude-SearchBotTraining crawler versus the index behind Claude's cited search answers.
- Claude-User vs Claude-SearchBotTwo Claude agents that both serve live answers, at different stages of the request.
- Google-Extended vs GoogleOtherNeither is Googlebot, and only one of them is an AI training control.
- PerplexityBot vs Perplexity-UserPerplexity's index crawler versus its live fetch on behalf of a searcher.
- Applebot vs Applebot-ExtendedApplebot powers Siri and Spotlight; Applebot-Extended is purely the Apple Intelligence training opt-out.
- Meta-ExternalAgent vs Meta-ExternalFetcherMeta runs one crawler for training data and another for user-triggered link fetches.
- GPTBot vs ClaudeBotThe two biggest AI training crawlers, compared on documentation, IP verification, and what blocking each actually costs.
- GPTBot vs CCBotBlocking GPTBot does not stop your content reaching OpenAI, because Common Crawl is a separate upstream source.
- GPTBot vs BytespiderOne documents its IP ranges and honors robots.txt; the other does neither.
- ClaudeBot vs CCBotAnthropic's own crawler versus the open dataset that also feeds model training.
Work with these bots, not just read about them:
- robots.txt Generator — build per-bot allow/block rules for all 28 crawlers at once.
- AI Bot Log Analyzer — see which of these bots actually visit your site.
- The complete guide to AI crawlers — background reading on how these bots differ.
Use the data in your own project:
This directory is published as an open dataset under CC BY 4.0 — grab it as JSON or CSV. Attribution appreciated; a link back to this page is plenty.

report.summary: A maintained open directory profiles 28 AI crawlers, detailing robots.txt behavior, IP ranges, and copy-paste allow/block rules for major model providers.
report.background: AI companies now deploy many crawlers for training, search indexing, and live user-triggered fetches. Website owners face confusing user agents, unclear opt-out controls, and robots.txt rules that may be ignored. The directory responds to this opacity by cataloging each bot's purpose, compliance status, and technical identifiers. It also clarifies that blocking a training crawler may not block live ChatGPT or Claude fetches, and that Common Crawl remains a separate upstream source. As publishers, developers, and platforms debate consent and compensation, this open dataset aims to make AI crawling more transparent and actionable.
key_points: The directory covers 28 crawlers from OpenAI, Anthropic, Perplexity, Google, Apple, Meta, ByteDance, Amazon, and others. Each profile explains what the bot does, whether it respects robots.txt, and provides copy-paste allow or block rules. Compliance is categorized as respects, partially respects, ignores, or unknown.

It highlights commonly confused pairs such as GPTBot versus ChatGPT-User and ClaudeBot versus Claude-User. Training crawlers and user-triggered fetchers are separate agents, so blocking the wrong one can have the opposite effect from what a site owner intends.

The project publishes IP ranges and an open dataset under CC BY 4.0 in JSON and CSV formats. This lets developers integrate crawler data into firewalls, log pipelines, analytics, and automated robots.txt generation.

Companion tools include an AI Crawler Access Checker, a robots.txt Generator for all 28 crawlers, and an AI Bot Log Analyzer. These help site owners audit current permissions and see which bots actually visit.

The monthly refresh and explanatory profiles address fast-changing AI crawler behavior, making it a practical reference for publishers, security teams, and developers who need current bot signatures and opt-out details.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this directory pressures crawler operators toward clearer documentation and predictable compliance. For developers, it provides structured data for blocking, monitoring, or allowing bots at scale. For publishers and regular users, it clarifies that robots.txt alone may not control AI training or live retrieval, and that separate agents require separate rules. The open dataset could become a shared reference for log analysis, CDN rules, and consent tooling. However, it does not resolve legal debates around fair use or compensation; it simply makes the technical landscape more legible and auditable.
report.tools: Start with the directory itself and its JSON/CSV dataset for scripts and dashboards. Use the robots.txt Generator to create per-bot rules, the AI Crawler Access Checker to audit current permissions, and the AI Bot Log Analyzer to identify real visits. Related projects to watch include Cloudflare AI Audit, Dark Visitors, and open-source log parsers that can match AI user agents and IP ranges.
